newsitem.title: USA: Flood waters rising in North Dakota, new warnings sounded.
newsitem.headline: Flood waters rising in North Dakota, new warnings sounded.

text.p: City officials appealed for volunteers and urged residents to reinforce sandbag dikes late Monday amid indications that flooding on the Red River in Fargo and areas nearby was far from over.

At Breckenridge, Minnesota, upstream from Fargo on the Red River, more evacuations were under way. Officials there said it appeared massive amounts of water were still flowing towards that town and ultimately would pass through Fargo.
Fargo Mayor Bruce Furness said "We think there is still three days of (rising) water south of us. If we can get by three days we think it will have passed us but we don't know for sure."
Students from North Dakota State University were being asked to volunteer to help shore up low and leaking dikes and Furness said any remaining dikes that are substandard will have to be built up.
Fargo's public works director, Pat Zavaral, said the city's permanent levee system as well as sandbag dikes were holding up well but he urged residents to make reinforcements.

Warmer spring weather melting a winter's accumulation of snow added to the runoff as did a break in a dike along a tributary of the Red south of Fargo. The river rose to 37.8 feet (11.52 metres) on Monday, topping Saturday's crest of 37.6 feet (11.46 metres), after a slight drop Sunday that forecasters had expected to continue.
There was some confusion Monday as to whether gauges had accurately recorded the weekend river levels, but the National Weather Service said it believed the new 37.8 feet reading was correct.
Both readings were more than 20 feet (6.09 metres) over flood stage and the highest recorded since a destructive flood of 1897.

There was more bad news Monday with a decision to start releasing water from Lake Traverse, a reservoir on the Minnesota-South Dakota border which empties into the Boise de Sioux River, a tributary of the Red. The lake reservoir is brim-full and hydrologists said they had had no choice.
The release will send more more water to the Red River Valley and could cause problems for the Breckenridge area.

At Gardner, North Dakota, a crossroads village north of Fargo, residents lost a fight to save Nora Church, a 1913 edifice founded by one of the oldest Norwegian Lutheran congregations in the state. They opened basement windows to let floodwaters in after moving possesions upstairs.
The nearby graveyard was under water.
"Right now we don't really anticipate any significant drop in the river for three or four days," Dennis Walaker, director of operations at the Fargo Public Works Department, said.

The Sheyenne River, which feeds into the Red north of Fargo, burst through dikes south of the city this weekend, merging with the Wild Rice River, which flows into the Red south of Fargo. Earthen and sandbag dikes built as temporary barriers to hold back the water will be tested longer than expected, Walaker said.

Residents fled some towns north of Fargo in anticipation of flooding along the Red and its tributaries as high water drains northward towards Canada. Emergency crews said ice on the Red slowed its flow north, backing water into tributaries and creating additional flooding along these waterways.

In the Minnesota towns of Perley and Hendrum, about 15 miles north of Fargo, most residents had evacuated. Dikes around these towns of about 150 people have held, John Korzeniowski, spokesman for the Norman County, Minnesota, Flood Management Team, said. The Red forms the Minnesota-North Dakota border as it flows northward to Winnipeg.
In Grand Forks, about 75 miles north of Fargo, residents prepared for the Red to crest later this week at 50 feet -- a foot higher than previoously forecast and more than 21 feet above flood stage.
"We've filled about 1.3 million sandbags and have about another 700,000 to go," said Rick Coulter, acting Emergency Management Officer in Grand Forks, a city of 71,000.

Two of three bridges connecting Grand Forks to East Grand Forks, Minnesota, may have to be closed this week, Coulter said. The Point Bridge in downtown Grand Forks would close when the river reaches 44.3 feet and the Sorlie Bridge, also downtown, would close when the river hits 46.75 feet.
